title: Should Trump set up an AI sovereign wealth fund?
gist: An analysis of proposals from Bernie Sanders and Donald Trump for the US state to capture AI-boom wealth via a sovereign wealth fund, arguing the scheme may be a poor bet on unprofitable, circularly financed AI firms and, worse, could hand those firms regulatory protection by aligning the government’s incentives with their success.

insights.claim: In June 2026 Senator Bernie Sanders proposed a bill levying 50 per cent of AI companies’ value, paid to the US government in shares, on the logic that AIs are built on the nation’s collective cultural production.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: A concrete equity-capture mechanism that, if advanced, would materially dilute AI-company cap tables.
insights.locator: In June 2026, the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders

insights.claim: Trump publicly backed the idea of AI firms 'giving back something to the public', promising the public would 'become very rich', an unusual convergence with Sanders on redistribution.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Bipartisan-sounding support raises the tail probability of a US state stake in AI firms becoming policy.
insights.quote: the public will become very rich

insights.claim: In Trump’s second term the US government has taken significant holdings in Intel, Global Foundries, US Steel and companies involved in rare-earth mining and quantum computing.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Signals an active state-equity precedent that makes an AI stake more plausible—watch for holdings in named firms.
insights.locator: In Trump’s second term, his government has taken

insights.claim: Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global, established in 1990 from petroleum revenues, now manages well over $2 trillion—more than $390,000 per citizen—and owns more than 2 per cent of all European shares, the biggest owner in that market.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: The benchmark for what a commodity-funded sovereign fund can accumulate—and the scale of market ownership it implies.

insights.claim: Economists across the spectrum warn that because the US runs a deficit, any sovereign wealth fund would be funded by going further into debt rather than by a surplus or windfall.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: A debt-financed fund changes the risk calculus—leveraged bets on volatile AI equities rather than surplus recycling.
insights.locator: And while economists from left and right

insights.claim: The 'Magnificent Seven' now represent roughly a third of the S&P 500’s value, up from just over a fifth in 2022, meaning most market gains of the past four years are concentrated in AI-related stocks.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Quantifies index concentration risk—the market’s returns are hostage to a handful of AI-exposed names.

insights.claim: The Magnificent Seven are profitable, but not from their AI businesses per se—Apple from phones, Microsoft from software, Amazon from everything—implying AI itself is not yet the profit engine.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Undercuts the premise that a fund would be buying into a self-sustaining AI profit stream.
insights.locator: The Magnificent Seven are all profitable

insights.claim: In 2025 Nvidia invested $100bn in OpenAI, which committed to spend those funds buying millions of Nvidia chips—a circular economy that obscures whether AI is booming or sums are just moving between balance sheets.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Flags vendor-financing circularity as a reason to distrust headline AI revenue growth.
insights.quote: This circular economy makes it difficult to determine whether AI is booming, or whether huge sums are simply being shifted from one balance sheet to another.
insights.locator: The most curious of the bunch is Nvidia

insights.claim: OpenAI and Anthropic have attracted tens of billions in revenue while spending hundreds of billions on compute and energy, and Anthropic’s claimed profitable Q2 2026 is met with scepticism as pre-IPO accounting.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Warns that pre-IPO AI profitability claims may not survive scrutiny—relevant to valuing the coming listings.
insights.locator: As OpenAI and Anthropic prepare to go public

insights.claim: Sam Altman has proposed handing 5 per cent of OpenAI to a US sovereign wealth fund and suggested Anthropic, Meta and Google do the same.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: The AI-side eagerness to give equity is itself a tell about what the firms expect in return.
insights.locator: This also might explain why Sam Altman

insights.claim: Zuckerman argues that if the US held large stakes in AI firms it would gain a strong disincentive to regulate them—so Altman may see 5 per cent as cheap insurance against regulation or a ban on Chinese rival models.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: The core contrarian read: the fund functions as regulatory protection, not public benefit.
insights.quote: Altman may see 5 per cent as a bargain price if it buys him insurance against regulation
insights.locator: If the US government held hundreds of billions

insights.claim: Zuckerman cites Norway as precedent for the capture risk: while environmentally progressive, its fund maintains a commitment to 'not dismantle but develop' fossil fuels and still issues Arctic oil and gas licences.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Historical evidence that state fund-holders become reluctant to bite the hand that feeds them.
insights.locator: This is one of the major dangers

insights.claim: US workers earned almost $12 trillion in 2024, so even a small fraction of income displaced by AI would quickly outpace the wealth an AI boom could generate to replace it.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Shows the fund is likely too small to cushion an AI employment shock—key to sizing any UBI or transition scheme.
insights.locator: US workers earned almost $12 trillion in 2024

insights.claim: Studies of AI disruption project 50 per cent or greater job loss in categories such as programmers, web designers and court reporters.
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: Names the white-collar categories most exposed to near-term AI displacement.

insights.claim: Zuckerman’s bottom line is that any idea uniting Trump, Sanders and Altman is likely too good to be true, and the fund is best understood as a way for AI firms to fend off regulation—'maybe even as a bribe.'
insights.speaker: Ethan Zuckerman
insights.so_what: The article’s investable takeaway: read the fund as an AI-industry regulatory hedge, not public wealth-building.
